articles.title: Texas’s AI Law: Before Deployment
articles.reader: Private employers and AI procurement teams
articles.decision: Identify applicable AI, privacy and biometric duties
articles.evidenceBoundary: Enacted and current codified Texas law and official implementation guidance checked October 12, 2026. The retailer example is hypothetical. HB149 business-sandbox intake was not verified; the federal-policy discussion is not a comprehensive preemption or litigation review.

sources.label: HB149, enacted enrolled text
sources.note: Enacted text; §10 sets January 1, 2026 effectiveness. Sections 2–3 amend biometric and processor-security provisions. Earlier introduced and committee versions are not the enacted authority.

sources.label: Business & Commerce Code Chapter 551: definitions and applicability
sources.note: Current codified text of §§551.001–.003. Source date denotes effectiveness, not the date this live code page was published.

sources.label: Business & Commerce Code Chapter 552: duties, prohibitions and enforcement
sources.note: Statutory thresholds, operator distinctions, disclosure timing, investigative powers, cure, penalties and liability provisions. Does not establish a judicial interpretation of contested terms.

sources.label: Business & Commerce Code Chapter 541: Texas Data Privacy and Security Act
sources.note: Current codified scope, definitions, rights, controller and processor duties, contract terms, assessments, exemptions and enforcement. HB149 amended §541.104(a).

sources.note: Commercial capture, notice and consent, retention, penalties, AI training and security exclusions, and subsequent non-exempt commercial use. Biometric identifier differs from the biometric data definition in Chapters 541 and 552.

sources.label: Business & Commerce Code Chapter 553: AI regulatory sandbox
sources.note: Statutory program framework, agency approvals, duration, reporting and limits on waivers. An enacted framework does not establish that intake is currently available.

sources.label: Consumer AI Rights: official TRAIGA overview
sources.publisher: Texas Office of the Attorney General
sources.note: Current public guidance and complaint route, including explicit healthcare-provider disclosure and government-only social-scoring and biometric provisions. Statutory text controls precise thresholds.

sources.label: AI in Texas: implementation of the 89th Legislature’s laws

sources.note: Primary announcement of recommendations to Congress. The announcement itself is not an enacted preemption statute, final rule or Texas-specific court order.

claims.claim: HB149/TRAIGA is enacted and took effect January 1, 2026; introduced bills and committee substitutes are historical proposals rather than the enacted text.
claims.qualification: The article does not import risk classifications or assessment duties from earlier bill versions.
recheck: Amendment or repeal of the relevant code provisions
Applicable final court order changing enforceability

claims.claim: The AI definition includes machine-based inference generating content, decisions, predictions or recommendations. Texas applicability has three alternative connections; consumer excludes commercial or employment context. Developer and deployer roles are defined separately.
claims.qualification: Consumer exclusions do not establish an exemption from provisions addressed to a person. Out-of-state headquarters alone does not resolve scope.
recheck: Authoritative interpretation of develops or deploys in this state

claims.claim: Governmental agencies offering AI intended to interact with consumers must disclose the AI interaction before or at interaction; disclosure must be clear, conspicuous, plain-language and free of dark patterns, may use a hyperlink, and is required even if AI is obvious.
claims.qualification: This is not a blanket disclosure duty for every ordinary private-business chatbot. The chapter uses governmental agency in §552.051 and defines governmental entity in §552.001; a specific institution's classification requires attention to the exact text.
recheck: Official interpretation of agency scope or disclosure implementation

claims.claim: An AI system used in relation to healthcare service or treatment triggers provider disclosure to the recipient or personal representative by the first service/treatment date, with disclosure as soon as reasonably possible in an emergency. The AG's current overview expressly identifies this provider duty.
claims.status: enacted and effective; supported by current official guidance
claims.qualification: Healthcare disclosure is not extinguished merely because a provider has a HIPAA-based TDPSA exclusion. Exact deployment scope and recipient notice require interpretation; no claim that every healthcare administrative tool has been judicially classified.
claims.locator: Requirements Under The Act Include: Disclosure to Consumers
recheck: Interpretation of AI used in relation to service or treatment

claims.claim: TRAIGA contains distinct intent-based harmful-use and constitutional-rights prohibitions, governmental social-scoring and biometric provisions, and specified illegal sexual-material/minor-impersonation provisions.
claims.qualification: Preserve intentionally aims in §552.052, sole intent in §552.055 and §552.057(1), intentional development/distribution in §552.057(2), and governmental entity in §§552.053–.054(b). §552.054(c)'s link to §503.001 is separately mapped in ai-10. No claim that every persuasion, scoring, scraping or content-generation use is banned.
recheck: Amendments to intent thresholds or referenced Penal Code provisions

claims.claim: Section 552.056 prohibits intentional unlawful discrimination against a protected class; disparate impact alone is insufficient to prove intent under that section. The section contains insurance treatment and a federally insured banking compliance provision, while TDPSA duties separately address unlawful discrimination and risky profiling.
claims.qualification: The disparate-impact rule is section-specific; no claim that outcomes are lawful under other laws. Insurance exception and banking compliance rule do not exempt those entities from all TRAIGA provisions.

claims.claim: TDPSA scope requires the statutory Texas connection, personal-data processing/sale, and generally a business outside SBA's small-business definition. Small businesses must obtain prior consent to sell sensitive data. Entity and data exclusions must be evaluated separately, including employment-context exclusions.
claims.qualification: The statute includes specified government, GLBA, HIPAA, nonprofit, higher-education and utility exclusions; the article is a scope summary, not a determination of a particular entity's SBA or sector status. TRAIGA has no analogous SBA threshold.

claims.claim: Covered controllers have data minimization, security, disclosed-purpose, consent, notice and consumer-rights duties; significant-decision profiling opt-out and specified processing-risk assessments can be relevant to AI workflows. Profiling is defined as solely automated personal-data processing evaluating or predicting personal aspects.
claims.qualification: Assessment duties depend on processing activities and risk, rather than all AI purchases. The financing example is hypothetical and conditional; no claim that all staff-approved recommendations constitute solely automated profiling.
recheck: Changes to profiling definitions or rights
Actual workflow changes affecting automation and significant decisions

claims.claim: HB149 expressly adds AI-system personal-data security to a processor's assistance duty. TDPSA processing contracts have specified terms, and controller/processor role is fact-based; neither role's liability is transferred away by the relationship.
claims.status: enacted and effective; HB149 amendment effective 2026-01-01
claims.qualification: Procurement table is a recommended ownership allocation. The statute does not universally require all listed vendor materials to be filed before every AI purchase. Training for a vendor's independent purposes prompts role review rather than an automatic classification.
recheck: Guidance on controller versus processor classification

claims.claim: Amended biometric law contains specified AI training/development and security exclusions, a unique-identification limit, a public-media consent clause with an individual-publication exception, and consequences for subsequent non-exempt commercial use. A §503.001 violation also violates TRAIGA §552.054(c).
claims.qualification: Biometric identifier in §503.001 differs from biometric data in Chapters 541/552. The individual-publication exception is not described as unconditional permission for any biometric processing. Subsequent-use clause specifically mentions possession, destruction and penalties.
recheck: AG or court interpretation of unique identification or subsequent use

claims.claim: The AG has principal/exclusive Chapter 552 enforcement subject to the licensing-agency provision; there is no private right of action under the chapter. A qualifying online complaint can lead to a civil investigative demand for the categories of information listed in §552.103.
claims.status: enacted and effective; official complaint link observed
claims.qualification: The article describes authorized investigative categories, not routine public filings. It makes no assertion that no investigations or enforcement actions exist, and does not exclude causes of action independently arising under other law.
recheck: Public enforcement action or authoritative investigation guidance

claims.claim: TRAIGA has a 60-day notice/cure framework and statutory penalties of $10,000–$12,000 for each court-determined curable violation or statement breach, $80,000–$200,000 for each uncurable violation, and $2,000–$40,000 per continued-violation day. Licensing sanctions require a violation finding and AG recommendation and may include up to $100,000. TDPSA uses a separate 30-day cure and up to $7,500 per violation.
claims.qualification: The TRAIGA cure requires correction, written statement, supporting documentation and necessary internal policy changes before the 60th day. TDPSA's statement also includes notifying the consumer where contact information is available. Do not collapse daily penalties, per-violation penalties or the two statutes' cure periods.
recheck: Court findings defining violation units or curability

claims.claim: TRAIGA's liability provisions address another person's prohibited use, discovery through specified processes, a rebuttable reasonable-care presumption, and no civil-penalty action under §552.105 for a system not deployed. Framework compliance alone does not establish the statutory discovery condition.
claims.status: enacted and effective; framework conclusion is textual interpretation
claims.qualification: Section 552.105(e)(2)(D) ties substantial recognized-framework compliance to an internal review process discovering a violation. No blanket NIST immunity claim, no assertion that adopting an untested policy establishes substantial compliance, and no claim of a judicial ruling on these defenses.
recheck: Changes to statute or referenced recognized frameworks

claims.claim: Chapter 553 requires DIR and applicable-agency approval, provides up to 36 months of testing/deployment with possible good-cause extension and quarterly reporting, preserves Chapter 552 Subchapter B requirements, and does not waive federal law. DIR separately reports government Chapter 219 adoption; its current SB1964 public-sector sandbox page says participation details will be published when available.
claims.status: Statutory framework enacted/effective; implementation observations verified 2026-10-12; HB149 business intake unresolved
claims.qualification: Public-sector SB1964 and HB149 business regulatory sandboxes are not interchangeable. Observed future-publication language is not proof of the status of every DIR initiative or private-business intake channel. Actual approval and waiver scope must precede reliance.
recheck: DIR publishes HB149 intake rules or application
